originalGroup.material:
A. Saturday bicycle check

The school bicycle club will hold a bicycle check on Saturday morning, from 9:00 to 11:30. Bring your bicycle to the covered area behind the sports hall. Please do not leave it at the main door, because another club needs that entrance.

Club members will help you check your tyres, brakes and lights. They can show you how to add air to a tyre, but they cannot replace broken parts. If your bicycle needs new parts, they will give you a note to take to a repair shop. You do not need to buy anything at the event.

Students under twelve must come with an adult. Each check takes about fifteen minutes. There is no booking system, so please join the line when you arrive. The last new check will begin at 11:15.

Bring your own helmet if you would like advice about how it fits. The club has no helmets for sale or loan. Heavy rain will not cancel the event because the area has a roof. However, strong winds may make it unsafe; check the school website after 8:00 before setting off.

B. A longer way to school

For two years, Ravi walked to school along Market Road. It was the shortest route, but every morning he had to wait at three busy crossings. When roadworks closed part of the road, his neighbour suggested a path beside the river.

Ravi thought the new route would take much longer. On the first day, he left home ten minutes early. The riverside path was longer, but it had only one crossing. He reached school five minutes earlier than usual.

The next day, Ravi took a small notebook. He wrote down when he left home and when he arrived. He did this for a week, including one wet morning. The new walk usually took twenty minutes, compared with twenty-five on Market Road. On the wet day, however, the river path was muddy, and he needed thirty minutes.

After the roadworks ended, Ravi did not always choose the same route. On dry days, he enjoyed the river path. After heavy rain, he used Market Road, where the pavement stayed firm.

His neighbour asked if he had found the best way to school. 'I've found two useful ways,' Ravi replied. 'Now I look out of the window before I choose.' A route could be longer on the map but quicker to walk, and the weather could change that again.

originalGroup.sourceNotice: 2026-10-24新题批次 b012；原创候选，非高考真题；自审及程序检查，不声称独立教师或学生稳定性验证。
originalGroup.material:
A. Two seed pots

Sofia planted two bean seeds for a school project. She put each one in a pot with the same kind of soil. Both pots stood beside the kitchen window, and she gave them the same amount of water. She labelled them A and B.

After four days, a green shoot appeared in Pot A. Nothing showed in Pot B. Sofia wanted to dig up B to see what had happened, but her brother suggested waiting. 'You may hurt it if it has already started growing under the soil,' he said.

Instead, Sofia recorded what she could see. Each morning she drew the pots and measured the shoot in A. Three days later, a shoot appeared in B too. It was smaller, but it looked healthy.

At school, Sofia's friend asked which seed was better. Sofia looked at her diary. 'A appeared first,' she said. 'But I don't know yet which plant will grow taller.'

She continued the diary for another two weeks. Sometimes A grew faster; sometimes B did. Her teacher liked the dates beside the drawings. Without them, the pictures would have shown two plants, but not how their growth had changed over time.

B. A note in a library book

When Owen borrowed a mystery story, a small piece of paper fell from between its pages. On it someone had written, 'Check the train time on page 64.' Owen wondered whether the note would give away the ending. He put it aside and started reading.

Halfway through the book, a detective asked how a visitor could be in two towns on the same evening. Owen remembered the note. He looked at page 64 and found a station timetable mentioned in a conversation. It helped him understand an important clue, but it did not tell him who had committed the crime.

When Owen returned the book, he showed the paper to the librarian. She explained that a reading group had discussed the story the previous month. One member sometimes wrote notes to remember questions for the meeting. The paper had probably been left behind by accident.

'Can I add my own note for the next reader?' Owen asked. The librarian smiled but gave him a different idea. The library had a review board where readers could leave comments without putting paper inside books. Owen wrote, 'Watch the small details. One ordinary conversation may matter later.' He did not mention the page number. He wanted the next reader to enjoy finding the clue too.

questions.prompt: Why did Owen leave out the page number in his review?
questions.material:
B. A note in a library book

When Owen borrowed a mystery story, a small piece of paper fell from between its pages. On it someone had written, 'Check the train time on page 64.' Owen wondered whether the note would give away the ending. He put it aside and started reading.

Halfway through the book, a detective asked how a visitor could be in two towns on the same evening. Owen remembered the note. He looked at page 64 and found a station timetable mentioned in a conversation. It helped him understand an important clue, but it did not tell him who had committed the crime.

When Owen returned the book, he showed the paper to the librarian. She explained that a reading group had discussed the story the previous month. One member sometimes wrote notes to remember questions for the meeting. The paper had probably been left behind by accident.

'Can I add my own note for the next reader?' Owen asked. The librarian smiled but gave him a different idea. The library had a review board where readers could leave comments without putting paper inside books. Owen wrote, 'Watch the small details. One ordinary conversation may matter later.' He did not mention the page number. He wanted the next reader to enjoy finding the clue too.
questions.explanation: The final sentence states his wish that the next reader enjoy discovery. No numerical ban, memory failure or wish to discourage readers is described.
